summary: Link-local IPv6 addresses need a zone identifier (such as an interface name) to say which network link they belong to. This document explains how users should type that identifier into user interfaces such as address fields. It replaces RFC 6874 and updates RFC 4007, RFC 7622 and RFC 8089.

eli5.summary: Some house numbers repeat on every street, so you must also say which street you mean. This tells software how people should write that extra street name next to an address.

subtitle: How people should type an IPv6 link-local address together with the interface it lives on.

tldr.problem: A link-local IPv6 address only makes sense together with a zone identifier such as an interface name, but many user interfaces give people no way to enter one.
tldr.mechanism: Any UI that accepts a non-global IPv6 address MUST let the user enter a link-local or scoped multicast address and pick a zone identifier. It SHOULD accept the RFC 4007 form such as fe80::1%eth0, with fallbacks if that is impractical.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9844 obsoletes RFC 6874 and does not apply to URIs fetched by web browsers.

today: RFC 9844 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2025. It obsoletes RFC 6874 and updates RFC 4007, RFC 7622 and RFC 8089. It states that its requirements do not apply to URIs fetched by web browsers.

sections.title: Zone Identifiers on Addresses
sections.content:
Many tools let a user type in an IPv6 address. RFC 4007 extends the text form of limited-scope addresses, such as link-local unicast and scoped multicast addresses, so that a zone identifier can be attached to the address. RFC 5952 does not mention this extension.

A zone identifier has purely local meaning inside the node that defines it, and is usually the same as the IPv6 interface name. It is meaningless to any other node. Examples are fe80::1234%eth0 on a Linux host and fe80::4321%7 on a Microsoft Windows host. Socket calls such as getaddrinfo() already accept this form.

Devices whose network stack does not support the human-readable zone identifier model of RFC 4007 are out of scope.
sections.eli5: An address like fe80::1 can exist on every cable plugged into your computer. The zone identifier is the cable's name, so the computer knows which one you mean.

sections.title: Why Users Need to Type Them
sections.content:
The RFC lists several cases where a person must enter a link-local address with its zone:

  • Debugging with a command like ping fe80::1234%eth0 on a host with more than one active link interface.
  • Configuring a device that only has a link-local address, such as a home router that cannot be reached at fe80::1%eth0 if the tool refuses zone identifiers.
  • Telling a network sniffer which link-local address on which interface to watch.
  • Microsoft Web Services for Devices (WSD) virtual printer ports, which can show an address whose zone identifier is not recognized by the software.
  • The NMEA OneNet marine networking standard, which uses IPv6 link-local addresses exclusively.

The RFC stresses that a complete address should be copyable from one UI to another. Strings like fe80::8d0f:7f26:f5c8:780b%enx525400d5e0fb are long, so anything except cut-and-paste is highly error prone.
sections.eli5: Imagine copying a very long secret code by hand. It is much safer to copy and paste it, so the box must understand the whole code, including the street-name part.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Documents
sections.content:
RFC 4007 says zone identifiers are text strings with no stated maximum length or syntax. The operating system maps the text to a numeric interface index, usually inside the socket API. Most systems also accept the interface number written as a decimal integer, which RFC 4007 recommends but does not require.

Some systems support a default zone identifier, but others, including Linux, do not. On Linux a link-local address without a zone index cannot be used in the socket API, so a UI solution matters there.

RFC 9844 obsoletes RFC 6874, which web browser implementors found impracticable to support. That reverts RFC 6874's change to the URI syntax of RFC 3986. It also updates RFC 7622 and RFC 8089 by deleting their references to RFC 6874, and updates RFC 4007 by adding the new UI requirement.
sections.eli5: An older rulebook tried to put the street name inside web addresses, and web browser makers said that was too hard. This new rulebook drops that idea and only talks about the boxes people type into.

sections.title: What a User Interface Must Do
sections.content:
A UI that allows or requires entry of an IPv6 address other than a global unicast address MUST provide a means to enter a link-local address or a scoped multicast address and to select a zone identifier as specified by RFC 4007, typically an interface identifier from the operating system.

The UI SHOULD support the complete RFC 4007 format, for example fe80::1%eth0. If that is impossible for practical reasons, it MAY use another delimiter in place of %; the hyphen is suggested, as in fe80::1-eth0. If that is also impossible, it MAY offer two input fields, a list of active zone identifiers, or a separate command-line parameter.

The program stores the address and zone identifier and converts the zone to an interface index, typically through the socket API. A faulty zone identifier is detected at that point and should be reported to the user as an error. A string such as fe80::1%eth0 cannot be parsed by POSIX inet_pton(). It must go through getaddrinfo(), or be split into two strings and handled with inet_pton() and if_nametoindex().

The recommendations in this document do not apply to URIs fetched by web browsers, because treating the zone identifier as part of the HTTP origin model is still unresolved.
sections.eli5: If a box accepts addresses, it has to let you say which cable you mean. The best way is to write the cable name after a percent sign, but boxes may use a dash or give you a second little box if needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Zone identifiers are of local significance only and must not be sent on the wire. Software that obtains a zone identifier through a UI should not transmit it further, and per RFC 4007 should not trust packets that carry textual non-global addresses as data.

RFC 4007 sets no limit on the length of a zone identifier and does not restrict its characters. A UI should therefore apply a length limit, typically the host operating system's limit on interface names, to reduce the risk of a buffer overrun. It should also check characters; for example, it should not allow ASCII NUL characters in the string.
sections.eli5: The street name is only for your own computer, so do not shout it across the network. Also, do not let someone type a name so long that it spills out of the box.
